newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia Krasnoyarsk aluminium majority owners unite.
newsitem.headline: Russia Krasnoyarsk aluminium majority owners unite.

text.p: A majority group of shareholders at Russia's Krasnoyarsk aluminium smelter, one of the world's largest, said on Thursday they would work together to end bickering to enact a cost-cutting programme.

A statement signed by officials who said they represented companies owning a total 57 percent of stock in the primary aluminium plant said collective action was needed to overcome quarrels to put the smelter on firmer financial ground.

"Full mutual understanding has been achieved between the participants of this group and there are no political disagreements, which previously had threatened to disrupt the resolution of those problems which had arisen," said the statement, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters.

The Krasnoyarsk smelter, also known as KrAZ, in southern Siberia, produced 780,000 tonnes of primary aluminium last year, or 28 percent of total output in Russia, which was the world's largest aluminium exporter and second biggest producer in 1996.
The statement represents efforts by some shareholders to unite and carry out financial revamping at the smelter, hit by rising production costs.
The moves would not affect production, said one of the statement's signatories, Dmitry Bosov.

But Bosov, who said he represented five companies -- Trans-World Metals of Britain and Russian companies Devisal, Kassana, Russian Investors and Elerak -- with a collective 11.2 percent stake in KrAZ, said shareholder accord was needed.
"A clear economic recipe for the factory is needed," he said by telephone from Krasnoyarsk. "We first and foremost need to work according to economic principles to cut costs."
Other signatories to the statement included representatives of unknown companies the Tanako financial-industrial group (20 percent), Level (10 percent) and Land (10 percent), Bosov said.

Glencore AG of Switzerland and Daewoo Corp each hold five percent in Krasnoyarsk, Bosov said, adding that those companies had not signed the statement because it had been prepared so quickly. The two companies could not be immediately reached for comment.
Bosov said a 20 percent stake was owned by unknown companies Kreb and Sitl, while Leo Trust Company had 7.9 percent.
He said Krasnoyarsk alone among Russian aluminium smelters had wage arrears of two and a half months and owed around $250 million to suppliers, employees and the budget.
Former Glencore employee Igor Vishnyevsky was appointed chief executive officer of the smelter earlier this month.
